posts.title: Herb five: Koromiko
posts.about: Herb of the week post introducing koromiko, the fifth of the eleven herbs, and its place in the Relief range.
posts.headline: Koromiko: the herb grandmother knew
posts.subline: Herb five of eleven, in our Relief range
posts.caption:
Koromiko grows almost everywhere in Aotearoa, from roadside banks to the edge of the bush. Ask an older Kiwi and there is a good chance they remember it.

It is a native hebe, with long narrow leaves and white to lilac flower spikes in summer. In rongoā Māori the leaves were traditionally used for upset stomachs, and on the skin for cuts and sores. During the Second World War, families even sent dried koromiko to soldiers overseas.

We use koromiko in our Relief range, the rub, spray and roll-on we make for everyday aches, bumps and bruises.

Herb five of eleven. Save this for the full set.

Did your nan know koromiko? Tell us below.

posts.title: Backyard cricket warm-up
posts.about: Christmas Day Reel teaching a 20-second warm-up before backyard cricket, the summer injury moment everyone recognises.
posts.headline: The Christmas cricket warm-up nobody does
posts.subline: Twenty seconds before you bowl your first over

shots.shot: Backyard lawn, wheelie bin as the wicket, tennis ball rolling across the grass
shots.text: Christmas Day cricket. Warm up first.

shots.shot: An uncle in jandals doing slow arm circles, small to big
Walking lunges across the lawn with a gentle twist over the front knee
shots.text: 6 walking lunges each side, with a twist

shots.shot: Side shuffles along the fence line, then a few easy run-ups
shots.text: Side shuffles, then three easy run-ups

shots.shot: First ball bowled gently underarm, then the next one faster
Wide shot of the whole family playing, laughter, long shadows

posts.caption:
Most backyard cricket injuries happen in the first over. Cold muscles, a big lunch and one heroic dive.

Twenty seconds is all it takes:
1. Ten arm circles each way, small to big.
2. Six walking lunges each side, with a twist.
3. Side shuffles across the lawn, then three easy run-ups before you bowl flat out.

It matters most for anyone who has not played since last summer, or who has an old shoulder or knee that likes to complain. Start slow, then build up.

If you go down hard and something swells fast, or you cannot put weight on it, get it checked by your GP or an after-hours clinic.

Save this for Christmas Day and send it to whoever bowls first.

posts.title: Boxing Day recovery guide
posts.about: Educational Boxing Day post from the dehydration blog article; it carries the day's one-day offer on Facebook.
posts.headline: Is your Boxing Day ache actually thirst?
posts.subline: A simple recovery guide for the day after

steps.t: A big glass when you wake, then sip all day. Electrolytes if you sweated.
A gentle walk or swim gets blood moving through tight, tired muscles.
Massage a little rub into sore spots, then sleep. Sleep does the real work.

posts.caption:
Muscle aches the day after Christmas are often less about the cricket and more about the heat, the sun and the extra glass of bubbles. Even mild dehydration can leave muscles feeling tight, crampy and sore.

Our Boxing Day recovery order:
1. Water first. A big glass when you wake, then keep sipping. Add electrolytes if you sweated a lot.
2. Then move. A slow walk or a swim beats a day on the couch.
3. A rub before bed. Massage a little of your X-ZONE rub into the sore spots, then get a proper sleep.

If cramps are severe, or you feel dizzy, confused or are barely needing the loo, see your GP or call Healthline on 0800 611 116.

The full article is on our blog, link in bio.

posts.title: Paddling shoulders on the beach
posts.about: Surf-season Reel teaching a 30-second shoulder mobility routine on the sand before paddling out.
posts.headline: Paddling shoulders: 30 seconds on the sand
posts.subline: Mobility before the first set

shots.shot: Board on the sand, surfer rolling their shoulders, waves breaking behind
Big slow arm circles facing the sea
Hands clasped behind the back, chest lifting, eyes closed
Lying on the board, pressing up slowly and lowering
shots.text: Press up on the board, 5 slow reps

shots.shot: On hands and knees in the sand, one arm threading under the other
Surfer picks up the board and runs into the water
shots.text: Save this for your next surf

posts.caption:
Paddling is most of surfing, and paddling is mostly shoulders. The first long sessions of summer are when sore, pinchy shoulders turn up.

Thirty seconds on the sand before you paddle out:
1. Big slow arm circles, ten each way.
2. Clasp your hands behind your back and open the chest for five breaths.
3. Lie on the board and press up, five slow reps.
4. Thread the needle in the sand, three each side.

The same routine suits anyone whose shoulders stiffen up with age or an old injury, surf or no surf. At the end of the day, a rub massaged into the tops of the shoulders is a good way to finish.

Pain that wakes you at night, or a shoulder that will not lift, needs a check with your GP or physio.

posts.caption:
Pūriri grows in the forests of the upper North Island, and it flowers almost all year round. If you have seen kererū and tūī busy in one tree in midwinter, there is a good chance it was a pūriri.

In rongoā Māori, pūriri leaves were traditionally used in warm washes for sprains, aches and sore backs.

In independent lab tests (Trinity Bioactives), pūriri tincture reduced COX-2, an enzyme linked to inflammation, by 14.2%. That is an in-vitro result on cells, not a trial on people. We share it because you should be able to see the science behind what goes on your skin.

Pūriri is one of the herbs in our Sports range, alongside harakeke, kūmarahou, kōwhai and pukatea.

posts.title: The 10% rule for January
posts.about: New Year carousel explaining why January injuries happen and the 10% rule, tied to the week 6 blog article.
posts.headline: Why January injuries happen
posts.subline: Too much, too soon. The 10% rule.

slides.b: Too much, too soon. And the simple rule that helps. Swipe.
New year, new plan. We go from very little in December to every day in January. Muscles adapt in weeks. Tendons and joints take longer.
Increase your weekly total by no more than about 10%. Minutes, kilometres or kilos. Pick one measure and track it.
Walking 60 minutes a week now? Next week, 66. The week after, about 73. Slow feels silly. It works.
Every third or fourth week, drop back a little. Recovery is when the body actually gets stronger.
Pain that changes how you move, swelling, or pain at night means back off. If it lasts more than a week, see your GP or physio.
Start slow, stay consistent, look after the body you have. Our full 10% rule guide is on the blog.

posts.caption:
Most January injuries are not bad luck. They are too much, too soon.

The 10% rule is simple: increase your weekly training by no more than about 10%, whether that is minutes walked, kilometres run or kilos lifted. Muscles adapt quickly. Tendons, ligaments and joints take longer, and that gap is where the trouble starts.

It matters even more if you are coming back after years off, carrying an old injury or living with arthritis. Slow progress is still progress, and it keeps you out on the track.

If pain changes how you move, comes with swelling or lasts more than a week, see your GP or physio.

Save this, and send it to the friend with the big 2027 plans. Full guide on our blog, link in bio.

How you treat your body the night after a big day decides how you feel the morning after.

Dan here. People ask what I actually do after a long day on the tools or the trail, so I filmed it. Nothing fancy.
1. Water before anything else.
2. A hot shower. It loosens everything up and opens the pores, so a rub goes in better after.
3. A couple of minutes massaging Sports Rub into whatever is complaining. Usually calves and lower back.
4. Five minutes of stretching on the floor while the kettle boils.
5. Bed by ten. Mostly.

The massage matters as much as the rub. Rub it in, do not just rub it on.

weeks.theme: Back into it: DOMS and recovery science. Rātā

posts.title: DOMS explained
posts.about: Recovery science carousel on why soreness peaks two days later, tied to the week 7 DOMS blog article.
posts.headline: Why you hurt two days later
posts.subline: DOMS explained, without the jargon

slides.h: Why you hurt two days later
slides.b: DOMS explained, without the jargon. Swipe.
Delayed onset muscle soreness. The ache that builds 24 to 72 hours after exercise your body is not used to.
New or harder work causes tiny strains in muscle fibres. The repair, and the inflammation that comes with it, takes a day or two to peak.
Lactic acid clears quickly. Downhill walking, lowering heavy weights and new sports are the usual causes.
Gentle movement, water, protein, a good sleep and massage. Ease back in rather than stopping completely.
Sharp pain, swelling, soreness still getting worse after three days, or dark urine: stop and see your GP.
Joanna Sharpe, ultra-distance cyclist

posts.caption:
The soreness that turns up two days after a big session has a name: DOMS, delayed onset muscle soreness.

When you ask muscles to do something new or harder, tiny strains appear in the fibres. Repairing them, and the inflammation that comes with it, takes time, which is why day two often hurts more than day one. It is not lactic acid. That clears quickly.

What helps: keep moving gently, drink water, eat some protein, sleep well and massage the sore muscles. Massage is where a rub like our Sports Rub fits in.

If you have sharp pain, swelling, soreness that is still getting worse after three days, or dark urine, stop and see your GP.

Save this for your first week back.

posts.caption:
Rātā is the red-flowering tree of the New Zealand forest in summer, a close cousin of the pōhutukawa. Northern rātā often starts life as a seed high in another tree, sending roots down until it stands on its own.

In rongoā Māori, parts of the rātā were traditionally used, including the inner bark on wounds and the nectar for sore throats.

It matters to our Relief range because Relief is our everyday, first-aid range: the rub, spray and roll-on for bumps, bruises and the aches of an ordinary day. Rātā sits there with harakeke, horopito, kahikatea and koromiko.

posts.caption:
In August 2024, Trinity Bioactives, an independent contract lab, tested our three rubs on human macrophages. These are cells that are active in pain and inflammation.

In those lab tests, the Sports Rub reduced inflammation-associated cells by 54.1%, the Joints Rub by 48.1% and the Relief Rub by 42.7%. Two herbs were also tested against COX-2, an enzyme linked to inflammation: tūpākihi oil reduced it by 28.4% and pūriri tincture by 14.2%.

Dr Vanessa Ingraham reviewed the results, and her evaluation is on our blog. {INGRAHAM_SUMMARY}

The honest bit: these are in-vitro results on cells in a lab, not a clinical trial on people. We share them because you deserve to see the science behind what we make.

posts.caption:
Most pre-season injuries come from trying to do in two weeks what the body needs six weeks to build.

For rugby, netball and football players, and the parents and coaches behind them:
1. Build slowly. About 10% more each week. Fitness first, then contact and full sprints.
2. Warm up every time. Ten minutes of jogging, dynamic stretches and build-up runs.
3. Recover on purpose. Sleep, water, an easy day after big sessions, and massage the tight spots.

Any head knock, or a joint that swells fast, needs a proper check with a GP or physio before going back.

posts.caption:
A tight hamstring after sprints is common. A sudden, sharp pain at the back of the thigh is different: that one means stop, ice it and get it checked by a physio or GP.

For the everyday tight kind, here is how players use Sports Spray at training:
1. Spray onto clean, unbroken skin over the back of the thigh.
2. Massage it in for a minute, working upward.
3. Follow with a gentle stretch, never a forced one.

The spray suits a training bag because there is nothing to scoop out with muddy hands. Patch test first if you have sensitive skin.

posts.title: Turmeric and the Joints Rub
posts.about: Joint-pain carousel from the Golden Turmeric blog: turmeric inside, the Joints Rub outside, with Mavis and Pam's quotes for the Facebook audience.
posts.headline: Turmeric inside, herbs outside
posts.subline: The natural duo for stiff, sore joints

slides.b: The natural duo for joint pain, and why they make sense together. Swipe.
A spice with a long traditional use for joints. Its active compound, curcumin, is widely studied for its role in inflammation.
Our higher-strength rub, with four native herbs: tūpākihi, kūmarahou, pukatea and karaeo. Massaged in where it is stiff.
One is part of what you eat. One you massage in, right where it aches. Together, a simple natural daily routine.
On blood thinners or diabetes medication, or having surgery? Talk to your GP or pharmacist before taking turmeric supplements.
Mavis, Huntly
Pam, Balclutha

posts.caption:
If you live with stiff, sore joints, a natural routine works best when it comes from two directions.

Inside: golden turmeric has a long traditional use for joints, and its active compound, curcumin, is widely studied for its role in inflammation. A golden milk, or turmeric in your cooking, is an easy start.

Outside: our Joints Rub, the higher-strength rub in our range, made with four native herbs traditionally used for pain. Massage it into the stiff spots morning and night.

One quick check: if you are on blood thinners or diabetes medication, or have surgery coming up, talk to your GP or pharmacist before taking turmeric supplements.

Mavis from Huntly and Pam from Balclutha said it better than we can. Swipe to the end.

posts.title: Herb eight: Pukatea
posts.about: Herb of the week Reel for pukatea, the swamp forest giant traditionally used for pain, found in both the Joints and Sports ranges.
posts.headline: Pukatea: herb eight, the swamp forest giant
posts.subline: In our Joints and Sports ranges

shots.shot: Low-angle shot up a tall pukatea in wetland forest
Slow pan across huge buttress roots in still water
shots.text: Buttress roots, built for swampy ground

shots.shot: Close-up of the pale bark
shots.text: Bark traditionally used in rongoā for pain

shots.shot: Glossy, toothed leaves moving in the breeze
shots.text: A giant of the swamp forest

shots.shot: Joints Rub and Sports Rub side by side on moss
shots.text: In our Joints and Sports ranges

posts.caption:
Pukatea is a giant of New Zealand's swamp forests. It stands on great buttress roots, with breathing roots that help it survive in wet, waterlogged ground.

In rongoā Māori, pukatea bark was traditionally used as a remedy for pain, including toothache, and for skin sores.

It is one of the few herbs that sits in two of our ranges: the Joints Rub, for stiffness and long-term joint pain, and the Sports range, for warm-up and recovery.

Herb eight of eleven. Three to go.

Have you walked through a kahikatea and pukatea swamp forest? Tell us where.

posts.title: Heat or ice, answered
posts.about: Injury first aid post answering the most-asked DM question, heat or ice for muscle and joint pain, tied to the week 8 blog article.
posts.headline: Heat or ice? The honest answer
posts.subline: Depends what hurts, and how new it is

steps.t: Fresh sprain or knock, swelling, first 48 hours. Wrapped, 15 to 20 minutes.
Tight back, sore neck, old aches. Warmth helps them relax and move.
Morning stiffness often feels better warm. Hot, swollen joints prefer cool.

posts.caption:
Heat or ice? The honest answer is that it depends on how new the pain is.

Ice is for new injuries. A fresh sprain, a knock or anything swelling in the first 48 hours. Wrap it in a cloth and keep it on for 15 to 20 minutes, never straight on the skin.

Heat is for stiffness. A tight lower back, a sore neck, muscles that ache after a long day. Warmth helps them relax.

Joints are where it gets personal. Morning stiffness and arthritis often feel better with warmth. A joint that is hot, red and swollen usually prefers cool, and a sudden hot, swollen joint is worth a GP visit.

Never put heat on fresh swelling, and never fall asleep on a heat pack.

For the everyday aches in between, our rubs are made to be massaged in. Save this.
posts.shoot: Split image: a wrapped ice pack on an ankle, and a wheat bag across a lower back, both in natural light.

posts.headline: How long does a jar really last?
posts.subline: Proper use, honest maths, then the saving

steps.t: 1 to 5 ml per area, massaged in, not just rubbed on.
Up to five times a day for a stubborn spot.
A {JAR_SIZE} jar lasts about {WEEKS} weeks at daily use on one area.

posts.caption:
Most people underuse a rub. A tiny dab, rubbed on and forgotten, is not how it is meant to work.

Proper use looks like this: 1 to 5 ml on the sore area, massaged in for a minute or two, up to five times a day. It goes in best after a shower or training, when the pores are open. Patch test first if your skin is sensitive.

At daily use on one area, a {JAR_SIZE} jar lasts about {WEEKS} weeks. If you live with arthritis or long-term pain, that can mean running out right when you need it most.

So we made refills simple. Subscribe and your rub arrives every {INTERVAL}, with {SAVING} off every order. Marni from Auckland says X-ZONE "cannot be bettered."

posts.title: Dan's roll-on after the tools
posts.about: Unpolished how-to Reel: Dan uses the roll-on on a sore shoulder at the end of a day on the tools.
posts.headline: Roll-on, sore shoulder, end of the day
posts.subline: Dan, straight off the tools

shots.shot: Dan at the ute tailgate, dusty, rolling his shoulder (Dan's voice: 'Long day overhead. Shoulder's had enough.')
Close-up: roll-on over the top and back of the shoulder
Dan's fingers massaging in small circles
Slow arm circles beside the ute
Roll-on tossed into the toolbox, lid shut

posts.caption:
Overhead work is hard on shoulders. Ceilings, gutters, painting, pruning: hours with your arms above your head leave the muscles around the shoulder tight and tired.

At the end of the day:
1. Roll it over the sore area, the top and back of the shoulder.
2. Massage it in with your fingers for a minute. Rub it in, not just on.
3. Finish with slow arm circles to loosen things off.

This is Dan, straight off the tools. Real and unpolished.

If your shoulder catches with pain, will not lift above your head, or the ache wakes you at night, see your GP or physio.

The roll-on lives in Dan's toolbox, and it fits in a handbag too.
